raw_response.country: Sub-Saharan Africa (cross-national sample: abstract states 30 nations, Sample section lists 32 nations, and regression tables report 31 countries: Angola, Benin, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Cote d'Ivoire, Comoros, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Sudan, Swaziland, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe)

criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1: The study investigates cross-national determinants of infant mortality in Sub-Saharan Africa rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. National average access to an improved water and sanitation source is included only as one control/mediating independent variable predicting infant mortality and is never studied as a dependent variable or service-access phenomenon in its own right.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines macro-institutional and governance variables—specifically per-capita IMF structural adjustment lending arrangements and Freedom House political rights/civil liberties democracy scores—so it would pass a broad macro-governance reading in the abstract (though even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall study decision is still exclude because it fails Criteria 1 and 4, as infant mortality is the sole outcome). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no' because aggregate cross-national IMF structural adjustment loan volume per capita and national democracy scores represent macro-financial/macro-governance background rather than a specific legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3: Quantitative cross-national longitudinal empirical analysis using two-way fixed effects ordinary least squares (OLS) and two-way fixed effects instrumental variable regression models on panel data from 1990, 1995, 2000, and 2005 (N = 70 country-year observations across 31 countries in Tables 1 and 2).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: The sole dependent/outcome variable reported across all empirical models (Tables 1 and 2) is the national infant mortality rate (probability of dying between birth and age 1 per 1,000 live births). Although the abstract states that structural adjustment affects infant mortality indirectly via access to an improved water and sanitation source (among seven variables), the authors never regress water or sanitation access on IMF structural adjustment; instead, they enter access to an improved water and sanitation source alongside HIV prevalence, caloric intake, and immunization rate as explanatory predictors of infant mortality and infer partial mediation from attenuation of the IMF coefficient on infant mortality. No water or sanitation access outcome is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies Criterion 5 for its own health research question: Unit of analysis and population (Sub-Saharan African nation-years, 1990-2005), exposure (logged per-capita IMF structural adjustment lending), outcome (infant mortality rate per 1,000 live births), and study design (two-way fixed effects OLS and IV panel regressions) are clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies Criterion 6: Full text is in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: The dependent variable in this analysis is the infant mortality rate

The main independent variable in the analysis is amount of money received from the IMF to a Sub-Saharan African nation in a given year as part of a Standby Arrangement Loan, Extended Fund Facility Arrangement Loan, Structural Adjustment Facility Arrangement Loan, or Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility Arrangement Loan.
We also include the average level of access to an improved water and sanitation source in our models.
TABLE 1 Fixed Effects Regression Estimates of Infant Mortality in Sub-Saharan African Nations

raw_response.exposure: International Monetary Fund (IMF) structural adjustment lending (logged amount of money received per million population under Standby, Extended Fund Facility, Structural Adjustment Facility, or Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility arrangements), alongside national covariates including HIV prevalence, average access to an improved water and sanitation source, caloric intake, immunization rate, democracy, public health expenditures, female secondary school enrollment, debt service, multinational corporate investment, international trade, GDP per capita, and domestic investment
raw_response.outcome: Infant mortality rate (probability of a child dying between birth and age 1 per 1,000 live births)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Country-year panel of Sub-Saharan African nations observed in 1990, 1995, 2000, and 2005 (70 observations across 31 countries in Tables 1 and 2; 30 mentioned in abstract and 32 listed in Sample section)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E04 - Wrong outcome; also fails C1 and narrow C2). The study's sole empirical outcome across all regression models (Tables 1 and 2) is the national infant mortality rate per 1,000 live births. National average access to an improved water and sanitation source is used strictly as an independent/control variable predicting infant mortality (entered simultaneously with HIV prevalence, caloric intake, and immunization rate to check attenuation of the IMF coefficient on infant mortality) and is never modelled or reported as an outcome. In addition, the primary exposure—aggregate per-capita IMF structural adjustment loan volume—does not examine a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing water or sanitation service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification; even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it reports no water or sanitation access outcome.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-national longitudinal panel study using two-way fixed effects OLS regression and two-way fixed effects instrumental variable regression
